title: Under Custody
description: Monthly snapshot data of incarcerated individuals under custody starting June 2014.
whatsincluded:
Monthly snapshot data of incarcerated individuals under custody starting June 2014. The dataset enumerates the number of people incarcerated at DOCCS facilities on the first of each month and includes information on the demographics of each incarcerated individual in addition to their facility, commitment county, crime of conviction, and parole board eligibility. 
    To ensure compliance with Correction Law §9 and to align with the New York State Committee on Open Government's advisory opinion on case FOI-AO-18823, CANY has deidentified the source data by (1) removing the names and departmental identification numbers of the individuals in custody, (2) sharing only a selection of the fields available in the source data, and (3) altering select fields to be less granular (for example, changing “date of birth” to “age range”).
howitsgenerated: This data is derived from DOCCS’ incarcerated individual movement system, which the agency employs for operational purposes, including transfers.CANY obtains the data through a monthly data-sharing agreement with DOCCS.
limitations: Because this dataset consists of snapshot data, rows representing the same individuals will be repeated from month to month. The data does not include individuals who are adjudicated as youth or individuals who are housed in DOCCS facilities as incarcerated parolees.
whypublish: By making this information publicly available, CANY seeks to promote a shared understanding of basic questions regarding the incarcerated population in New York State: How many people are incarcerated in the state? Where are they incarcerated? What are the characteristics of the individuals who are incarcerated? What charges were they convicted of? And how have these answers changed over time?

title: OMH Self-Harm
description: Data compiled by the Office of Mental Health (OMH) regarding incidents of self-harm with monthly data starting in 2020 and annual starting in 2014.
whatsincluded:
The dashboard below includes statistical data compiled by the Office of Mental Health (OMH) regarding incidents of self-harm, suicide attempts, and deaths from suicide. OMH defines self-harm as 'self-injurious behavior with a nonfatal outcome with no evidence (either explicit or implicit) that the person intended to die.' OMH defines suicide attempt as 'self-injurious behavior with a nonfatal outcome accompanied by evidence (either explicit or implicit) that the person intended to die, which may require medical and/or security intervention to reduce likelihood of death or serious injury.' Lastly, OMH defies suicide as 'self-injurious behavior with a fatal outcome accompanied by evidence (either explicit or implicit) that the person intended to die.'
Data on self-harm is monthly starting in 2020, data on suicide attempts is monthly starting from January 2014, and data on suicides is annual starting in 2014.
howitsgenerated: OMH classifies incidents based on clinical assessment and review of documentation from both OMH and the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision (DOCCS). In some cases, OMH consults with the Central New York Psychiatric Center (CNYPC) Suicide Prevention Department. Final classifications are reviewed and compiled by the OMH Suicide Prevention Workgroup (SPWG).
limitations: OMH and DOCCS maintain separate classification systems for self-injury, the numbers shown here are from OMH. Although DOCCS may defer to OMH’s clinical determinations in some cases, it does not revise Unusual Incident Repoorts (UIRs) to reflect those reclassifications, resulting in discrepancies in the number of incidents between the two data sources. For suicides, OMH and DOCCS classifications typically align.
whypublish: By making this information publicly available, CANY seeks to promote a shared understanding of basic questions regarding the incarcerated population in New York State: How many instances of self-harm, suicide attempts, and completed suicides occurred across New York State prisons? What facilities did these incidents take place in? Which methods were used? And how have these answers changed over time?

title: Releases from Custody
description: This dataset is a derivative of DOCCS' Releases dataset and contains data from January 2016 to the present. It represents data associated with incarcerated individuals only; incarcerated parolee releases, youthful offenders, and court-ordered discharges are excluded. The dataset represents release transactions, not individuals released. If an individual is released or discharged multiple times on the same incarceration sentence, multiple records will be included in the dataset. The dataset includes information on the demographics of each individual released in addition to the assigned facility at release, commitment county, release type, and agency released to (if applicable).
whatsincluded: Covers people released or discharged from DOCCS custody starting January 2015. Only individuals incarcerated in DOCCS facilities are included — releases of incarcerated parolees, youthful offenders, and court-ordered discharges are excluded. Each row is a release transaction rather than a person, so someone released more than once within the same sentence appears more than once. Fields cover the released individual's demographics along with their facility at release, county of commitment, type of release, and (where applicable) the agency they were released to.
howitsgenerated: Sourced from DOCCS' internal movement-tracking system, which the agency uses for operational purposes such as transfers. CANY receives this data monthly from DOCCS. Because Correction Law §9 limits how long release records may be retained and shared (as of a November 2024 update), each monthly file DOCCS provides only contains release transactions from roughly the prior three years; CANY stitches together just under a year of new data from each file to build a continuous record running from January 2016 forward. To comply with Correction Law §9, an advisory opinion from the state Committee on Open Government (case FOI-AO-18823), and New York's data privacy statutes including the Clean Slate Act, CANY strips names and DIN numbers, publishes only a subset of the available fields, and coarsens some fields (for example, date of birth becomes an age range).
limitations: This is not a full count of every DOCCS release or discharge — it reflects only what's in the files DOCCS shares with CANY, subject to the exclusions above (youth adjudications, court-ordered discharges, and incarcerated parolees are all left out). Any corrections DOCCS later makes to historical records won't be reflected here, since the dataset isn't retroactively refreshed.
whypublish: CANY publishes this to give the public a basic picture of who is leaving DOCCS custody, from where, under what circumstances, and how that has shifted over time.

title: Unusual Incident Reports
description: An unusual incident report can include multiple incidents; this dataset is structured to have one row per incident. DOCCS defines an unusual incident in Directive 4004 as a serious occurrence that (1) may impact upon or disrupt facility operations, or (2) has the potential for affecting the Department’s public image, or (3) might arouse widespread public interest. In general, any incident shall be reportable under the provisions of this directive which (1) satisfies the definition (above) of ’unusual incident,’ or (2) involves use of chemical agents, or (3) involves staff use of a weapon, or (4) results in moderate or serious injury to any incarcerated individual/releasee or staff. More detail about these reports can be found in DOCCS' Directive 4004.
whatsincluded:
Tracks unusual incidents at DOCCS facilities starting in January 2014. DOCCS Directive 4004 defines an unusual incident as a serious occurrence that could disrupt facility operations, affect the department's public image, or draw significant public attention — covering things like assaults, staff use of weapons, contraband, deaths, disruptive behavior, accidents, escapes, self-harm, and suicide attempts. The directive also requires reporting of any incident involving chemical agents, staff weapon use, or moderate-to-serious injury, regardless of whether it fits the general definition; the full incident-category list and reporting rules are in Appendix A of the directive.

Two things worth knowing before using this data: first, incident counts here won't exactly match DOCCS' own internal totals or annual reports, partly because some incidents CANY receives through FOIL are redacted and some may still be pending approval when CANY's quarterly request is processed (DOCCS' 2023 annual report counted 16,060 incidents that year versus 16,048 shown here, a difference under 0.01%). Second, counts may not line up with figures from other agencies because of differing reporting standards — for instance, death counts here can differ from those reported by the State Commission of Correction. See Limitations below for more.
howitsgenerated: Per Directive 4004, facility staff phone incidents in to DOCCS' Communications Control Center, which logs them in a computerized reporting system. The directive and an accompanying manual set reporting deadlines and required narrative and documentary content. A single report can cover more than one incident tied to the same event; these can be grouped using the facility log number, CCC number, and incident date-time fields. Sample source reports that CANY obtains through FOIL are available for reference.
limitations:
The two main caveats are (1) this dataset likely undercounts incidents relative to DOCCS' own internal figures, and (2) differing reporting rules mean incident counts here won't always match other DOCCS datasets or external agencies' records.

Shifts in reported incident volume over time may reflect changed reporting policy rather than a real change in incident rates. For example, DOCCS altered how it counted drug contraband incidents in August 2021, requiring outside lab confirmation before counting a find as an unusual incident, and reported contraband incidents dropped sharply afterward — though it's hard to separate how much of that drop reflects the policy change versus an actual decline in contraband found.

Some incident codes only appear in more recent years of data. Narcan use, for instance, isn't recorded before 2019, even though DOCCS facilities have operated under a statewide standing order for Narcan since at least 2015; earlier uses likely weren't categorized as unusual incidents under the reporting rules of the time.

Staff use of force can show up three different ways in this data: a report-level flag, an incident-level flag, and a distinct 'staff use of weapons' incident type. The two flag-level fields capture force more broadly, including force without a weapon, so they give a fuller picture of use of force than the narrower weapons-incident category shown on the dashboard; the processed data available for download allows comparison across all three.

Incidents tied to Central Office or Community Supervision aren't shown on the dashboard, but are present in the underlying source and processed data.
whypublish: This dataset gives the public visibility into out-of-the-ordinary occurrences inside correctional facilities and how often they happen, which is useful for spotting patterns or shifts over time, whether at a single facility or across the system.

title: Deaths in Custody
description: DOCCS data reporting the death of a person in custody compiled by the SCOC from M187 reports.
whatsincluded: A record of deaths in DOCCS custody starting January 2020, based on reports filed with the State Commission of Correction (SCOC). A death in custody is the death of anyone in DOCCS custody, whether it occurred at the facility itself or elsewhere, such as an outside hospital. Includes the deceased individual's demographics (age, gender, ethnicity, race), date of death, terminal incident location, and the facility they were assigned to at the time. CANY generalizes Date of Birth to Birth Year and Death Date/Time to Death Date to protect privacy.
howitsgenerated: Under 9 NYCRR §7022.4, DOCCS facilities must notify SCOC of an incarcerated person's death within six hours of pronouncement, followed by a detailed follow-up (M187) report on medical history and circumstances within ten days. SCOC compiles this data from those filings, and CANY receives it monthly under a data-sharing agreement with SCOC.
limitations: SCOC's data doesn't include cause or manner of death. CANY points to other sources for that information, including DOCCS' annual mortality reports and the Attorney General's Office of Special Investigation data tables, both linked below.
whypublish: This gives the public a baseline for tracking deaths in custody over time; paired with the individual-level reports linked below, it documents both how often deaths occur and the circumstances surrounding them.

title: Staffing Levels
description: An overview of budgeted and actual fill levels, in full-time equivalents, for staff positions at DOCCS facilities from 2022 to the present. This data is divided into four categories (security staff, health services, program services, support services), and fill levels for security staff are further divided by position (corrections officers, lieutenants, sergeants, captains, deputy superintendents, civilian security staff).
whatsincluded: Tracks budgeted versus actual staffing (in full-time equivalents) at DOCCS facilities from 2022 forward, broken into four categories — security, health services, program services, and support services — with security staff further broken down by role (corrections officers, sergeants, lieutenants, captains, deputy superintendents, and civilian security staff). Total fill levels, though not budgeted levels or category breakdowns, are also included for 2020 and 2021. Central Office, Community Supervision, and other non-facility staff aren't covered.
howitsgenerated: Figures from 2022 onward come from a biweekly staffing report produced by the DOCCS budget office, obtained by CANY through FOIL. The 2020-2021 figures come from separate facility fill-count reports that only tally total staff per facility, not staffing categories.
limitations: Fill levels and vacancy rates are only part of the picture — actual day-to-day staffing also depends on how many employees are out on workers' compensation, vacation, sick leave, or other absences, none of which this data captures.
whypublish: Staffing levels and vacancies shape how a facility actually runs day to day. CANY publishes this as a starting point for understanding DOCCS' staffing situation, while recognizing there's much more to the department's staffing challenges than what's visualized here.

title: Workers' Compensation
description: This data is from annual reports to the Workers' Compensation Board contains information on the number, type, cost, and outcomes of incidents filed by facility as well as the average number of Full Time Equivalents (FTE) at each facility during the fiscal year.
whatsincluded: Drawn from the annual New York State Government Employees' Workers' Compensation Claims reports for fiscal years 2019-2025 (which include records back to FY2015). Those reports cover work-related incidents reported to the Workers' Compensation Board and the New York State Insurance Fund (NYSIF) by Classified Service employees in certain Executive Branch agencies, including staff represented by CSEA, PEF, NYSCOPBA, Council 82, PBANYS, and Management/Confidential. This dataset narrows that down to DOCCS facilities only, and includes the number, type, cost, and outcome of claims by facility, plus each facility's average full-time-equivalent (FTE) staffing for the fiscal year.
howitsgenerated: Chapter 171, Section 7 of the Laws of New York (2007) requires the President of the NYS Civil Service Commission to file an annual report on workplace injuries, illnesses, and comp claims across Executive Branch agencies. The Department of Civil Service gathers incident data through its Accident Reporting System (ARS), while NYSIF supplies the claims data; incidents dated within the fiscal year (April 1-March 31) are counted through the following June 30 to reduce the effect of processing delays. FTE figures come from the Department of Civil Service's NYSTEP personnel system.
limitations: This data can be affected by underreporting, claims-processing delays, and inconsistency in how specific injuries get reported. When comparing facilities, account for differences in facility size and population makeup.
whypublish: DOCCS security staff, as Security Services Unit employees, receive more generous workers' compensation benefits than most state employees. Over the period covered, work-related incidents have risen sharply, adding pressure to DOCCS' existing staffing shortages and driving up costs to the state through both compensation payouts and overtime. CANY publishes this data to increase transparency around how the system is used, which it sees as necessary for spotting patterns of abuse and supporting reforms that protect both employees and taxpayers.

title: OMH Suicide Attempts
description: Data compiled by the Office of Mental Health (OMH) regarding incidents of suicide attempts, monthly data startin in 2014. Numbers do not align with DOCCS reports, OMH numbers may be higher.
whatsincluded: This dataset contains records of suicide attempts in DOCCS custody from January 1, 2014 to July 31, 2024 as reported by OMH. Note that the number of suicide attempts in this dataset may differ significantly from other data sources such as DOCCS' unusual incident data due to different reporting methods. Some facilities are split by unit and reported separately on different rows, reflecting the structure of the source data. To sum by facility, you can aggregate based on FACILITY_NAME. Please see the context statement above the dashboard for more detailed information. The source data was obtained from OMH through the Freedom of Information Act Law (FOIL)
howitsgenerated: OMH classifies incidents based on clinical assessment and review of documentation from both OMH and the Department of Corrections and Community Supervision (DOCCS). In some cases, OMH consults with the Central New York Psychiatric Center (CNYPC) Suicide Prevention Department. Final classifications are reviewed and compiled by the OMH Suicide Prevention Workgroup (SPWG).
limitations: OMH and DOCCS maintain separate classification systems for self-injury, the numbers shown here are from OMH. Although DOCCS may defer to OMH’s clinical determinations in some cases, it does not revise Unusual Incident Repoorts (UIRs) to reflect those reclassifications, resulting in discrepancies in the number of incidents between the two data sources. For suicides, OMH and DOCCS classifications typically align.
whypublish: By making this information publicly available, CANY seeks to promote a shared understanding of basic questions regarding the incarcerated population in New York State: How many instances of self-harm, suicide attempts, and completed suicides occurred across New York State prisons? What facilities did these incidents take place in? Which methods were used? And how have these answers changed over time?

Incarcerated individuals may be able to access this lifeline, depending on facility policy.

title: OMH Suicides
description: Data compiled by the Office of Mental Health (OMH) regarding incidents of suicide, monthly data startin in 2014.
whatsincluded:
The dashboard below includes statistical data compiled by the Office of Mental Health (OMH) regarding incidents of suicide, from suicide. OMH defines self-harm as 'self-injurious behavior with a nonfatal outcome with no evidence (either explicit or implicit) that the person intended to die.' OMH defines suicide attempt as 'self-injurious behavior with a nonfatal outcome accompanied by evidence (either explicit or implicit) that the person intended to die, which may require medical and/or security intervention to reduce likelihood of death or serious injury.' Lastly, OMH defies suicide as 'self-injurious behavior with a fatal outcome accompanied by evidence (either explicit or implicit) that the person intended to die.'
Data on self-harm is monthly starting in 2020, data on suicide attempts is monthly starting from January 2014, and data on suicides is annual starting in 2014.

title: Office of Mental Health (OMH) Caseload
description: Includes people receiving psychiatric services while incarcerated as reported to the CNYPC. Excludes informal, short term, DOCCS prescribed, and non-psychiatricic medication.
whatsincluded: Statistical data compiled by the NYS Office of Mental Health (OMH) on people receiving psychiatric services while incarcerated in DOCCS facilities. This entry covers the Facility Caseload Census — everyone on the OMH mental health caseload — as monthly data starting January 2022; it's drawn from the same combined OMH source as the Program Census dataset. Prescribed-medication figures only reflect psychiatric medications prescribed by OMH psychiatrists, not medications prescribed by DOCCS medical staff or non-psychiatric prescriptions.
howitsgenerated: Facility staff report caseload figures monthly to the Central New York Psychiatric Center (CNYPC), which compiles and aggregates them on OMH's behalf.
limitations: Medication counts shouldn't be read as a measure of overall treatment volume — they exclude DOCCS-prescribed and non-psychiatric medications. The data also only reflects people formally on the OMH caseload, not those receiving informal or short-term mental health support.
whypublish: CANY publishes this to give the public a shared basis for understanding the OMH population within DOCCS: what share of the incarcerated population is on the OMH caseload, their medication status and caseload designations, and how these figures have trended over time.

title: Office of Mental Health (OMH) Program Census
description: DOCCS OMH data regarding those housed in specialized mental health units (BHU, ICP, RMHU).
whatsincluded: Statistical data compiled by the NYS Office of Mental Health (OMH) on people receiving psychiatric services while incarcerated in DOCCS facilities. This entry covers the Program Census — people housed specifically in specialized mental health units, such as Behavioral Health Units (BHU), Intermediate Care Programs (ICP), and the Residential Mental Health Unit (RMHU) — as monthly data starting January 2022, drawn from the same combined OMH source as the Facility Caseload dataset. Everyone counted in the Program Census is also part of the broader OMH mental health caseload. Prescribed-medication figures only reflect psychiatric medications prescribed by OMH psychiatrists, not medications prescribed by DOCCS medical staff or non-psychiatric prescriptions.
howitsgenerated: Facility staff report program census figures monthly to the Central New York Psychiatric Center (CNYPC), which compiles and aggregates them on OMH's behalf.
limitations: Medication counts shouldn't be read as a measure of overall treatment volume — they exclude DOCCS-prescribed and non-psychiatric medications. The data also only reflects people formally on the OMH caseload, not those receiving informal or short-term mental health support.
whypublish: CANY publishes this to give the public a shared basis for understanding the OMH population within DOCCS: how many people are housed in specialized mental health programs, their designations, and how these figures have trended over time.
